title: Who does what now? Ministers explain the science, innovation and AI reshuffle
label: 21 October 2026 · Machinery of government changes
summary: Ministers and senior officials from the departments most affected by the abolition of DSIT explained why responsibilities were split, how they will co-ordinate on science, innovation, AI and digital, and how budgets, procurement and regionalisation will be handled. They repeatedly reassured that discovery science is protected, described procurement and social-value changes to favour UK industry, set out how AI strategy now sits at the Prime Minister’s office while departments keep operational ownership, and agreed to provide more transparency on costs and specific funding decisions (notably for UKRI and STFC).

glossary.definition: UK Research and Innovation, the public body that funds research and innovation in the UK.
Science and Technology Facilities Council, the UK agency running big physics facilities (like Diamond and ISIS).
Government-funded technology centres that help firms and researchers develop and scale innovations.
Government Digital Service, which sets digital standards and technical architecture for public services.
Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which now hosts the Prime Minister’s AI taskforce.
A technical label meaning spending counts as R&D under internationally accepted rules.

chapters.title: Why the departments were reshaped
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say the change aims to put science 'in the service of industry' and give AI a prime‑ministerial focus, while promising discovery science remains protected.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we're examining the recent split of DSIT into parts across Departments and what that means for science, innovation and technology scrutiny.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: Minister McDonald, why abolish the single department that signalled science was central? How will delivery and political leadership work now?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: The Prime Minister's brief to me was clear: put science in the service of industry. Form follows function—this structure aligns science, investment and trade to speed commercialisation.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: People fear a downgrading of blue‑sky research. Will core discovery budgets be protected?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: Yes. Discovery funding is protected; the aim is to capture more of the value here in the UK, not to cut curiosity‑driven science.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: Who's in charge in Cabinet when priorities clash?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: I sit in BIST and represent AI strategy at Cabinet through the OPMC. Trade-offs are worked through the Department and at Cabinet committees like the National Economic and National Security Councils.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Was this a policy-driven reorganisation or political? And stakeholders now don't know who to contact—how will you provide a clear single point of engagement?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: It was policy-driven—to fix long-standing commercialisation issues. We are mapping stakeholder contacts and will make clear who leads on what; large firms often want to engage across several Departments anyway.

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: On AI, we deliberately put the strategy in OPMC because it is cross-Government and strategic; many G7 partners are doing the same.

chapters.title: Budgets, procurement and backing British business
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say UKRI allocations for discovery haven't been cut, procurement rules will favour UK value through social value and national security exceptions, and Departments must be clearer about costs of the reshuffle.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: Alex, have the UKRI buckets changed after the £86bn announcements? Will discovery money be top-sliced for AI or defence?

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: The machinery change hasn't altered UKRI's budget split: roughly half still supports discovery. AI and scale-up investments have been drawn from the non-discovery buckets.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: What about the public cost of the reorganisation—will you publish it?

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: Departments are absorbing admin costs in their budgets and GIAA is reviewing processes. We'll provide what detail we can and commit to follow up on publication.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: If admin costs are absorbed, what is being cut elsewhere to pay for this reorganisation?

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: Mainly administrative reallocations, not R&D budgets; we'll come back on the precise lines where feasible.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: Procurement is the Government's biggest lever. How will you use it to back UK firms rather than default to big foreign suppliers?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: Procurement reforms include social value and national security levers. We want to maximise UK business benefit within international rules and are piloting ways to make SMEs easier to buy from.

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: For AI and chips we're using rapid procurements, advance market commitments and the sovereign AI scheme to create revenue certainty and keep companies here.

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: We're setting up a commercial innovation hub to help Departments buy innovation and bring together SMEs into proven solution catalogues for public buyers.

turns.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo
turns.text: SMEs tell me NHS procurement is harder than selling to the UN—repetitive paperwork and demands for bulk discounts. Will you fix that?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: Yes. NHS procurement can be hard for innovators; we will look at specific cases and work to simplify routes to market.

chapters.title: Devolution, clusters and UKRI money
chapters.takeaway: Ministers announced allocations to support regional innovation but said criteria, delivery and transparency will be worked out with local partners; some UKRI reprioritisation funds are earmarked for clusters.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What do the changes mean for regional R&D and the £500m local innovation pledge?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: Regionalisation is a Prime Minister priority. £270m of the local innovation partnerships fund will be placed with mayoral authorities and UKRI will direct about £1bn from its settlement to support world-leading clusters.

turns.speaker: George Freeman
turns.text: Will money go only to mayoral areas? How will you avoid political or academic capture and target places that can attract inward private investment?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: The goal is clusters of national or international significance; they may or may not be in mayoral areas. Criteria are being designed with UKRI and local partners; private investment is a key metric.

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: UKRI will use Frascati‑compliant R&D funding to back clusters. We are working with mayoral authorities to ensure genuine partnership and will publish more detail on how funds will be used.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: Who owns long-term capability for mid-TRL scaling—skills, testing facilities and institutions?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: BIST leads the industrial strategy and agencies like UKRI, Innovate UK and the British Business Bank are aligning to help firms scale, improve access to test facilities and back scale‑up finance.

chapters.title: AI: who leads, who regulates and who is accountable
chapters.takeaway: AI strategy and major cross‑Government projects sit in OPMC; departments keep operational ownership for sectoral AI. Ministers said safety, testing, defence and international cooperation are priorities, and they will consider legislation if needed.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: Ollie Ilott, what are the immediate priorities of the Prime Minister’s AI taskforce?

turns.speaker: Ollie Ilott
turns.text: Set the overall framework for Government on AI, build the central team, coordinate Departments and push immediate cross‑cutting work like the Ukraine data partnership.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: Who has the levers to ensure safety across health, justice and other sectors—can the taskforce make coherent policy across Departments?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: Strategy and prime‑ministerial direction sit in OPMC; Departments remain accountable for operational and sectoral AI decisions. The taskforce fills the gap for cross‑Government priorities and urgent projects.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: Is AI safety an explicit, funded priority? Will you audit and assure AI systems used by Government?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: Yes—testing capability has been strengthened via AISI and NCSC inputs, we are working on hardening public services and exploring assurance and insurance models; we will also convene internationally at G20 level.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lloyd
turns.text: DCMS will lead on copyright, misinformation, deepfakes and public sector digital transformation, while GDS handles technical standards and architecture.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Quickfire: who leads on AI regulation, cyber, standards and public-sector adoption?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: Overall strategic AI regulation sits with OPMC (me); sectoral regulation depends on the area—cyber is DCMS, public-sector adoption is GDS/DCMS, and departments own their specific contracts.

turns.speaker: Ollie Ilott
turns.text: Crucially, AI is a prime‑ministerial priority and that gives the taskforce the convening power to drive cross‑Government action.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Is there a risk of diffusion—too many places doing AI? How will industry know who to approach?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: We will make it clear: BIST leads AI‑producing sectors; DCMS leads digital/tech sector; the taskforce leads strategic cross‑cutting AI. We will clarify engagement routes for industry.

turns.speaker: Dr Gardner
turns.text: Will legislation be needed for AI?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: We are not ruling anything out. If legislation is needed to address risks, it will be considered; but many immediate levers are operational or regulatory.

chapters.title: STFC, life sciences and transparency requests
chapters.takeaway: Ministers defended protecting key physics facilities but acknowledged financial problems at STFC and committed to follow up on unclear shortfalls; life sciences oversight spans Health and BIST with procurement and data opportunities.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: What is happening at STFC and Harwell? We were told no cuts, yet staff and communities see closures. Who decides and will core facilities stay open?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: STFC must live within its budget. UKRI has allocated additional funding to stabilise it. The current plan intends to keep Diamond, ISIS, Muon and the Central Laser Facility operational while STFC fixes its financial control.

turns.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo
turns.text: I've had reports of a further £100m shortfall and confidentiality agreements for staff. Can you confirm?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: I asked to see that evidence. There are two simultaneous events—STFC reprioritisation and a UKRI voluntary severance programme—and that may be causing confusion. Provide me details and I'll validate and write back.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: On life sciences, will co‑ordination improve now you sit across Health and BIST—will this speed drugs from discovery to patients?

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: I now oversee the investment and science side across Health and BIST. OLS still links industry with MHRA and NICE regulators. We're shortening clinical trial timelines and seeking alignment so the UK is attractive for drug introduction.

turns.speaker: Emily Darlington
turns.text: How do you link basic research in AI, quantum and neuromorphic work so Britain keeps advantages in foundational technologies?

turns.speaker: Kanishka Narayan
turns.text: We have an AI for science strategy and a hardware plan that ties PhD support, ARIA investments and procurement together—aiming to build compute and chip capability here, with BIST and UKRI coordinating funding streams.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You agreed to return written details on: (a) the cost of the MOG changes, (b) what UKRI reprioritisation means in practice, and (c) clear confirmation and evidence on STFC commitments. That will be very helpful.

turns.speaker: Chris McDonald
turns.text: Yes. We'll supply more detailed information in writing and follow up on specifics the Committee requests.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Committee will continue scrutiny—this reshuffle raises important questions about coordination, transparency and safeguarding science while promoting UK commercialisation.
